title: Catherine of Alexandria (25 November)
hookLine: a learned martyr of legend, patron of students and philosophers

lines: A YOUNG WOMAN FACES AN EMPEROR.
cards: What would you do if an emperor called in his cleverest philosophers to argue you out of your faith, in public, with your life on the line? That's the scene at the heart of today's story.
A young woman of Alexandria, well read and well born, walks up to the emperor and tells him his persecution is wrong. He doesn't have her killed on the spot. He does something stranger.
He sends for the experts. Who wins? That's the story of Catherine of Alexandria.

teach.b: First, an honest word about the source. Catherine's story reaches us as a legend, a martyr's tale told and retold, and historians can't confirm its details.
The Church keeps her feast on 25 November and leaves that question open. What the legend gives us is a picture worth looking at.
The philosophers arrive ready to make short work of a girl. Catherine argues back, point by point.

And the debate ends the wrong way for the emperor: the philosophers themselves come over to her side, and they are put to death for it. Then the emperor tries to break her, literally, on a wheel studded with spikes.
The wheel shatters at her touch. In the end she is beheaded.

teach.h: A BROKEN WHEEL AND A BOOK.
teach.b: That's why paintings show her holding a broken wheel, and often a book. The book matters. Students and philosophers took her as their patron.
In her story, the courage comes out of her mind, not instead of it. A promise in Luke's gospel fits her well.
Jesus tells his followers that when they're dragged before kings and governors, they shouldn't rehearse their defense. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I will give you a mouth and wisdom."
Wisdom without courage stays home and thinks.

teach.h: FOR I WILL GIVE YOU A MOUTH AND WISDOM.
teach.b: Courage without wisdom charges in and says something foolish. She is remembered for having both at once: she thought hard, and then she said it out loud, to the one person in the room who could hurt her.

how: Saint Catherine of Alexandria is remembered on 25 November; schools, colleges and student groups named for her sometimes mark the day, and art shows her with a book and a broken wheel.

o: a martyr of legend who out-argued philosophers
an empress who freed Alexandria's Christians
a philosopher who taught an emperor's sons

games.q: you're Catherine. the emperor has gathered his cleverest philosophers to argue you down in public. what do you do?
o: stay silent and let them talk
games.why: in the legend she argues, and the experts brought in to defeat her end up on her side.

practice: Choose a question that's easy to avoid, the kind that gets pushed away because it's uncomfortable or tangled, and sit with it on purpose: what do you actually know, and what are you guessing? Don't try to solve it now.
If you pray, ask for wisdom, and for the courage to act on whatever you find; if you don't, let your mind stay with the question without running off.

wordCard.voice: Catherine. The learned young martyr of legend, shown with a book and a broken wheel, patron of students and philosophers.

carryVoice: Your line: wisdom and courage. In her story, the two always came together. Until tomorrow.
